notes:
1. Meaning of Lokayukta

  • Lokayukta is the State-level anti-corruption ombudsman.

It is established to inquire into allegations involving:

  • Corruption.
  • Abuse of power.
  • Maladministration.
  • Misuse of official authority.
  • It deals with specified public functionaries of a State.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lokayukta → State-Level Anti-Corruption Ombudsman

2. Meaning of the Term

The term consists of:

  • Lok → People.
  • Ayukta → Appointed authority or Commissioner.

Lokayukta therefore broadly means:

  • An authority appointed to protect public interest by promoting accountability in administration.

3. Nature of Lokayukta

Lokayukta is generally a:

  • Statutory Body.

It is established under:

  • State Lokayukta Act enacted by the respective State Legislature.

It is not a:

  • Constitutional Body.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Lokayukta → Statutory

Not → Constitutional

4. State-Level Institution

Lokayukta functions at:

  • State level.

Lokpal functions at:

  • Union level.

5. Need for Lokayukta

State Governments exercise wide powers relating to:

  • Administration.
  • Public services.
  • Welfare schemes.
  • Local Governments.
  • Public expenditure.

Therefore, an independent institution is required to examine allegations involving misuse of those powers.

6. Objectives of Lokayukta

Major objectives include:

  • Receiving complaints.
  • Inquiring into corruption.
  • Examining abuse of official position.
  • Addressing maladministration where permitted.
  • Promoting integrity.
  • Improving transparency.
  • Strengthening accountability.
  • Protecting public interest.
  • Encouraging ethical governance.

7. First Administrative Reforms Commission

The concept of Lokayukta emerged from recommendations of:

  • First Administrative Reforms Commission.

Year:

  • 1966.
📌 Must-Memorise

First ARC → 1966 → Lokpal + Lokayukta

8. Recommendation of First ARC

The First ARC recommended:

  • Lokpal at Union level.
  • Lokayuktas in States.

9. First State to Establish Lokayukta

The first State to establish a Lokayukta was:

  • Maharashtra.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Lokayukta State → Maharashtra

10. Maharashtra Lokayukta Law

Maharashtra enacted:

  • Maharashtra Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayuktas Act, 1971.

11. Beginning of Maharashtra Lokayukta

The institution began functioning in:

  • 1972.
📌 Must-Memorise

Maharashtra Act → 1971

Institution Functioning → 1972

12. Spread to Other States

After Maharashtra:

  • Several States enacted their own Lokayukta laws.
  • Structure and powers differ because each State uses its own legislation.

13. Central Act and Lokayukta

The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 primarily established:

  • Lokpal at Union level.

It also required States to establish:

  • Lokayuktas.

14. No Uniform State Structure

The 2013 Act does not prescribe one identical operational model for all State Lokayuktas.

States continue to determine through their own laws:

  • Composition.
  • Appointment.
  • Jurisdiction.
  • Powers.
  • Procedure.
  • Removal.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Lokpal → Uniform Central Law

Lokayukta → State-Specific Laws

15. State Lokayukta Acts

A State Legislature may regulate:

  • Composition.
  • Appointment.
  • Qualifications.
  • Jurisdiction.
  • Powers.
  • Inquiry procedure.
  • Removal.
  • Functions.

16. Variations among States

Lokayukta laws may differ regarding:

  • Number of Members.
  • Appointment procedure.
  • Public servants covered.
  • Chief Minister jurisdiction.
  • Investigative powers.
  • Recommendation powers.
  • Relationship with vigilance agencies.

17. General Role

Lokayukta generally:

  • Receives complaints.
  • Conducts inquiries.
  • Examines corruption allegations.
  • Examines abuse of authority.
  • Deals with maladministration where State law permits.
  • Recommends appropriate action.

18. Maladministration

Maladministration may include:

  • Delay.
  • Arbitrary decisions.
  • Abuse of discretion.
  • Unfair administrative action.
  • Negligence.
  • Misuse of authority.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lokayukta → May Cover Corruption + Maladministration, Depending on State Law

19. Public Interest

Lokayukta promotes public interest by ensuring:

  • Fair exercise of public authority.
  • Accountability of officials.
  • Impartial examination of complaints.
  • Administrative integrity.

20. Composition Varies

There is no uniform composition for all Lokayuktas.

Generally, the institution consists of:

  • One Lokayukta.

Some States additionally provide:

  • One or more Upa-Lokayuktas.

21. Lokayukta

The Lokayukta is:

  • Head of the institution.

The office supervises:

  • Complaints.
  • Inquiries.
  • Administration.
  • Recommendations.

22. Upa-Lokayukta

Upa-Lokayuktas may:

  • Assist Lokayukta.
  • Handle assigned cases.
  • Reduce pendency.
  • Improve disposal of complaints.

23. Number of Upa-Lokayuktas

The number of Upa-Lokayuktas:

  • Depends on respective State law.
  • Is not uniform across India.

24. Appointing Authority

Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta are generally appointed by:

  • Governor

under the relevant State Act.

📌 Must-Memorise

Lokayukta Appointment → Governor

25. Consultation Process

Depending on State legislation, consultation may involve:

  • Chief Minister.
  • Chief Justice of High Court.
  • Speaker of Legislative Assembly.
  • Leader of Opposition.
  • Chairman of Legislative Council, where applicable.

26. No Uniform Consultation Formula

The exact consultation process:

  • Varies from State to State.
  • Depends entirely on relevant State Lokayukta Act.

27. Governor vs Chief Minister

Governor:

  • Formal appointing authority under State law.

Chief Minister:

  • May participate in consultation where provided by State law.
  • Is not necessarily the appointing authority.

28. General Qualification Pattern

In many States, Lokayukta is appointed from persons who have held high judicial office.

Common examples include:

  • Former Supreme Court Judge.
  • Former Chief Justice of a High Court.
  • Former High Court Judge.

29. State-Specific Qualifications

Exact qualifications depend on:

  • State Lokayukta Act.

Therefore, TNPSC questions must distinguish:

  • General institutional pattern.
  • State-specific statutory provision.

30. Upa-Lokayukta Qualifications

Many State Acts may prescribe:

  • Judicial experience.
  • Administrative experience.
  • Other statutory qualifications.

31. Oath or Affirmation

Before entering office, Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta generally take:

  • Oath or affirmation.

The oath is administered before:

  • Governor.
  • Or another authority specified by State law.

32. Contents of Oath

The oath generally includes:

  • Faithfulness to Constitution.
  • Faithful discharge of duties.
  • Upholding law.

33. Tenure

Tenure varies across States.

Many State Acts prescribe:

  • Five years.
  • Or an upper age limit.
  • Whichever is earlier.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Lokayukta Tenure → Not Uniform Across India

34. Reappointment

Reappointment:

  • Depends on State law.

Several States restrict reappointment to strengthen:

  • Independence.
  • Neutrality.

35. Salary and Service Conditions

Salary, allowances and service conditions are determined by:

  • Relevant State Lokayukta Act.

36. Protection of Service Conditions

After appointment, service conditions are generally protected from:

  • Arbitrary alteration.

Purpose:

  • Preserve institutional independence.

37. Resignation

Lokayukta generally resigns by:

  • Written resignation to Governor.

38. Removal Authority

Lokayukta is generally removed by:

  • Governor

according to the procedure prescribed by the relevant State Act.

39. Common Grounds for Removal

Common grounds may include:

  • Misbehaviour.
  • Incapacity.
  • Insolvency.
  • Unsound mind declared by competent court.
  • Conviction involving moral turpitude.
  • Other statutory grounds.

40. Judicial Inquiry

Several State laws provide for an inquiry by:

  • High Court.
  • Or another judicial authority

before removal for misbehaviour.

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Lokayukta Removal Procedure → State-Specific

41. Vacancy

A vacancy may arise because of:

  • Completion of tenure.
  • Resignation.
  • Removal.
  • Death.
  • Attaining statutory age limit.

42. Acting Lokayukta

Some State laws permit:

  • Upa-Lokayukta.
  • Or another authorised person

to discharge Lokayukta functions during:

  • Vacancy.
  • Absence.
  • Inability to act.

43. Safeguards for Independence

Independence may be supported through:

  • Appointment by Governor.
  • Consultation with multiple constitutional authorities.
  • Fixed tenure.
  • Protected service conditions.
  • Statutory removal procedure.
  • Separate administrative establishment.

44. Purpose of Independent Appointment

A broad consultation mechanism seeks to reduce:

  • Arbitrary appointments.
  • Partisan control.
  • Executive domination.

45. Meaning of Jurisdiction

Jurisdiction means:

  • Persons.
  • Offices.
  • Matters

over which the Lokayukta has legal authority under State law.

46. Persons Generally Covered

Depending on State law, jurisdiction may extend to:

  • Chief Minister.
  • Ministers.
  • Members of State Legislature.
  • State Government officials.
  • Civil servants.
  • Officers of Local Bodies.
  • Government corporations.
  • Statutory bodies.
  • Other specified public authorities.

47. Chief Minister

Jurisdiction over Chief Minister:

  • Is not uniform.
  • Depends on State legislation.

Different States may provide:

  • Full jurisdiction.
  • Partial jurisdiction.
  • Exclusions.
  • Special procedures.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

CM under Lokayukta → Depends on State Law

48. Ministers

Most State Lokayukta laws may cover:

  • Ministers.
  • Former Ministers.

subject to:

  • State-specific statutory provisions.

49. Public Servants

Lokayukta jurisdiction may extend to:

  • State civil servants.
  • Government employees.
  • Public-authority officers.
  • Officials of Government-controlled bodies.

50. Definition of Public Servant

The definition depends on:

  • Applicable State Lokayukta Act.
  • Other relevant laws.

51. Matters Generally Covered

Lokayukta may deal with:

  • Corruption.
  • Abuse of official position.
  • Misuse of authority.
  • Maladministration.
  • Financial irregularities.
  • Misconduct.

52. General Powers

Depending on State law, Lokayukta may:

  • Receive complaints.
  • Conduct preliminary inquiry.
  • Order investigation.
  • Summon witnesses.
  • Require documents.
  • Examine records.
  • Recommend disciplinary action.
  • Recommend prosecution.

53. Complaint

Any person may generally submit a complaint:

  • In the manner prescribed by State law.

54. Contents of Complaint

A valid complaint generally includes:

  • Complainant details.
  • Identity of public servant.
  • Nature of allegation.
  • Supporting documents where available.

55. Frivolous Complaints

Frivolous or malicious complaints:

  • May be rejected according to law.

56. Preliminary Inquiry

Preliminary inquiry determines:

  • Whether complaint is maintainable.
  • Whether sufficient material exists.
  • Whether detailed investigation is necessary.

57. Purpose of Preliminary Inquiry

It acts as a:

  • Filtering mechanism

before full investigation.

58. Investigation

Where sufficient grounds exist, Lokayukta may:

  • Investigate directly where State law permits.
  • Or refer/direct investigation through an authorised agency.

59. Investigation Objectives

Investigation seeks to determine:

  • Whether misconduct occurred.
  • Whether evidence supports allegations.
  • Whether legal or departmental action is required.

60. Evidence Collection

Under applicable State law, the Lokayukta or authorised agency may:

  • Examine witnesses.
  • Call for records.
  • Inspect documents.
  • Obtain relevant information.

61. Search and Seizure

Search and seizure are generally carried out by:

  • Competent investigating authority

under:

  • Criminal procedure.
  • Applicable State law.

62. Lokayukta and Police Powers

The source notes that Lokayukta itself generally does not perform:

  • Ordinary police search operations.

63. Investigation Report

An investigation report may contain:

  • Facts established.
  • Evidence collected.
  • Findings.
  • Recommendations.

64. Recommendations

Lokayukta may recommend:

  • Departmental proceedings.
  • Disciplinary action.
  • Criminal prosecution.
  • Administrative reforms.
  • Corrective measures.

65. Recommendatory Nature

In many States:

  • Lokayukta recommendations are not themselves equivalent to a criminal conviction.

Implementation depends on:

  • Competent authority.
  • Relevant State law.

66. Departmental Proceedings

Lokayukta may recommend:

  • Departmental inquiry.
  • Suspension where legally authorised.
  • Disciplinary proceedings.

The competent authority proceeds under:

  • Applicable service rules.

67. Criminal Prosecution

Where evidence reveals criminal misconduct:

  • Prosecution may be initiated before competent court according to applicable law.

68. Lokayukta Is Not a Court

Lokayukta cannot:

  • Convict.
  • Acquit.
  • Award criminal punishment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lokayukta → Inquiry/Recommendation

Court → Conviction/Punishment

69. Criminal Trial

Criminal trial is conducted by:

  • Competent Criminal Court.
  • Special Court where applicable.

70. Lokpal and Lokayukta

Lokpal:

  • Union level.

Lokayukta:

  • State level.

Both are anti-corruption ombudsman institutions within their respective jurisdictions.

71. Separate Jurisdiction

Lokpal and Lokayukta have:

  • Separate jurisdiction.
  • Separate legal framework.
  • Separate administrative structures.

72. No Supervisory Control by Lokpal

The source states:

  • Lokpal does not exercise supervisory control over State Lokayuktas.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Lokpal ≠ Superior Authority over Lokayukta

73. State Vigilance Department

States may maintain institutions such as:

  • Vigilance Departments.
  • Vigilance Commissions.
  • Vigilance Directorates.
  • Anti-Corruption Wings.

74. Anti-Corruption Bureau

Several States have:

  • Anti-Corruption Bureau.

It may investigate:

  • Bribery.
  • Corruption.
  • Criminal misconduct.
  • Financial irregularities.

75. Lokayukta vs ACB

Lokayukta:

  • Independent statutory institution.
  • Receives complaints.
  • Conducts inquiries.
  • Makes recommendations.

ACB:

  • Investigating agency.
  • Collects evidence.
  • Investigates corruption offences.

76. Coordination with Vigilance Agencies

Lokayukta may:

  • Seek reports.
  • Obtain records.
  • Refer matters.
  • Coordinate investigation

according to State law.

77. Relationship with Police

Where a criminal offence is disclosed, investigation may involve:

  • State Police.
  • Anti-Corruption Bureau.
  • Special Investigation Units.

78. Relationship with Departmental Authorities

After inquiry, Lokayukta may recommend:

  • Departmental proceedings.
  • Disciplinary action.
  • Administrative reform.

79. Relationship with Courts

Lokayukta:

  • Is not a Court of Law.

Courts:

  • Conduct trials.
  • Convict or acquit.
  • Impose criminal punishment.

80. Annual Report

Many State laws require Lokayukta to submit:

  • Annual Report.
  • Special Reports where necessary.

81. Report to Governor

The report is generally submitted to:

  • Governor.

82. Legislature

Governor may place the report before:

  • State Legislature

according to the relevant State law.

83. Contents of Annual Report

An annual report may include:

  • Number of complaints.
  • Nature of allegations.
  • Recommendations.
  • Action taken.
  • Administrative observations.

84. Administrative-Reform Role

Lokayukta may also recommend:

  • Simplification of procedures.
  • Better supervision.
  • Improved transparency.
  • Stronger internal controls.

85. Lack of Uniformity

A major limitation is:

  • Different laws in different States.

Therefore, India has no completely uniform Lokayukta system.

86. Limited Jurisdiction

Some State laws exclude:

  • Certain constitutional authorities.
  • Certain categories of officials.
  • Certain administrative matters.

87. Recommendatory Powers

In many States:

  • Lokayukta primarily issues recommendations.
  • Final implementation depends on competent authority.

88. Delays

Inquiry may be delayed due to:

  • High complaint volume.
  • Limited staff.
  • Complex cases.
  • Administrative procedures.

89. Dependence on Other Agencies

Lokayukta may depend upon:

  • Vigilance agencies.
  • Police.
  • ACB.
  • Departmental authorities

for:

  • Investigation.
  • Evidence collection.
  • Implementation.

90. Resource Constraints

Some Lokayuktas may face:

  • Staff shortages.
  • Financial constraints.
  • Infrastructure limitations.
  • Technical limitations.

91. Low Public Awareness

Many citizens may not know:

  • Lokayukta jurisdiction.
  • Complaint procedure.
  • Remedies available.
  • Distinction between Lokayukta and ordinary grievance bodies.

92. Constitutional Position

Lokayukta is not expressly established by the Constitution.

However, constitutional provisions relating to:

  • Equality.
  • Accountability.
  • Responsible Government.
  • Financial control.
  • Rule of Law

support its functioning.

  • Fair investigation.

130. Core Difference

Lokpal:

  • Union-level institution.
  • Established under Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013.
  • Deals with specified Union public functionaries.

Lokayukta:

  • State-level institution.
  • Established under State legislation.
  • Deals with specified State public functionaries.

131. Uniformity Difference

Lokpal:

  • Uniform Central statutory framework.

Lokayukta:

  • State-specific framework.
  • Powers and composition vary.

132. Appointment Difference

Lokpal:

  • Appointed by President under Central statutory framework.

Lokayukta:

  • Generally appointed by Governor under State law.

133. Institutional Difference

Lokayukta:

  • Independent statutory institution.

State Vigilance Department:

  • Government department or vigilance/investigative structure within State administration.

134. Functional Difference

Lokayukta:

  • Receives complaints.
  • Conducts inquiries.
  • Makes recommendations.

Court:

  • Conducts judicial trial.
  • Convicts or acquits.
  • Awards punishment.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

What is Lokayukta? → State-level statutory anti-corruption ombudsman.

Is Lokayukta a Constitutional Body? → No.

What type of body is it? → Statutory Body.

Who recommended Lokayuktas? → First Administrative Reforms Commission.

In which year? → 1966.

What did First ARC recommend at Union level? → Lokpal.

What did it recommend at State level? → Lokayuktas.

Which was the first State to establish Lokayukta? → Maharashtra.

Which law did Maharashtra enact? → Maharashtra Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayuktas Act, 1971.

When did the institution begin functioning? → 1972.

Which Central Act requires States to establish Lokayuktas? → Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013.

Does that Act prescribe an identical Lokayukta structure for every State? → No.

Who determines composition and powers? → Respective State Legislature through State law.

Is Lokayukta structure uniform throughout India? → No.

What are the common areas of variation? → Composition, appointment, jurisdiction, powers, tenure and procedure.

Who is the head of the institution? → Lokayukta.

Who may assist Lokayukta? → Upa-Lokayukta.

Is an Upa-Lokayukta compulsory in every State? → No.

Who generally appoints Lokayukta? → Governor.

Can Chief Minister participate in the appointment process? → Yes, where State law provides consultation.

Can Chief Justice of High Court be consulted? → Yes, depending on State law.

Are Lokayukta qualifications identical across States? → No.

What is the common judicial qualification pattern? → Former Supreme Court Judge, former High Court Chief Justice or former High Court Judge, depending on State law.

Is tenure uniformly five years throughout India? → No.

What determines tenure? → State law.

To whom does Lokayukta generally resign? → Governor.

Who generally removes Lokayukta? → Governor under State statutory procedure.

Name common grounds for removal. → Misbehaviour, incapacity, insolvency, unsound mind and specified convictions.

Can a judicial inquiry be required before removal? → Yes, under several State laws.

What is jurisdiction? → Persons and matters over which Lokayukta may legally act.

Can Chief Minister be covered? → Depends on State law.

Are Ministers generally covered? → Often yes, subject to State law.

Are civil servants covered? → Usually specified categories are covered under relevant State Act.

What matters can Lokayukta examine? → Corruption, abuse of power, maladministration, financial irregularities and misconduct where law permits.

What is maladministration? → Unfair, arbitrary, delayed, negligent or improper administrative action.

Can Lokayukta receive complaints directly from citizens? → Generally yes, in the prescribed manner.

What is a preliminary inquiry? → Initial examination to determine whether complaint deserves detailed investigation.

What happens after sufficient material is found? → Investigation may be ordered or conducted according to State law.

Can Lokayukta summon witnesses? → State law may provide such power.

Can it call for official records? → Yes, where authorised by State law.

Who generally carries out search and seizure? → Competent investigating authority under applicable law.

Can Lokayukta convict an accused person? → No.

Who conducts criminal trial? → Competent Criminal Court or Special Court.

What can Lokayukta recommend? → Departmental action, disciplinary action, prosecution, administrative reform or corrective measures.

Are all recommendations automatically binding? → Not necessarily; it depends on State law.

What is Anti-Corruption Bureau? → State investigating agency dealing with corruption offences.

What is the difference between Lokayukta and ACB? → Lokayukta is statutory ombudsman/inquiry institution; ACB investigates criminal corruption cases.

Does Lokpal control Lokayukta? → No.

What is the difference between Lokpal and Lokayukta? → Lokpal operates at Union level; Lokayukta operates at State level.

What report does Lokayukta commonly submit? → Annual Report.

To whom? → Governor.

Where may the report then be placed? → State Legislature according to State law.

What are major limitations of Lokayukta? → Different State laws, limited jurisdiction, recommendatory powers, delays, staff shortages, dependence on other agencies and low public awareness.

Which Article guarantees Equality Before Law? → Article 14.

Which Article deals with State executive power? → Article 154.

In whom is State executive power vested? → Governor.

Which Article provides Council of Ministers to aid and advise Governor? → Article 163.

Which Article provides collective responsibility to Assembly? → Article 164(2).

Which Article regulates State Government business? → Article 166.

Which Article protects State Legislature privileges? → Article 194.

Can Lokayukta inquire into constitutionally protected legislative speeches and votes? → No, according to the source framework.

Which Article provides State Budget? → Article 202.

Which Article deals with Consolidated Fund? → Article 266.

Which Article protects property against deprivation except by authority of law? → Article 300A.

Which Article contains safeguards for civil servants? → Article 311.

Which case emphasised independent anti-corruption investigation? → Vineet Narain v. Union of India, 1997.

Which case introduced the principle of Institutional Integrity in vigilance appointments? → P.J. Thomas Case, 2011.

Which case dealt with prosecution-sanction delay? → Subramanian Swamy v. Manmohan Singh, 2012.

Which case is directly important for statutory nature and powers of Lokayukta? → Chandrashekaraiah v. Janekere C. Krishna, 2013.

Which case held FIR registration generally mandatory for cognizable offences? → Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh, 2013.

Which case struck down Section 6A of DSPE Act? → Subramanian Swamy v. Director, CBI, 2014.

Which case emphasised transparency in public-resource allocation? → Common Cause v. Union of India, 2017.

Which case dealt with criminalisation of politics? → Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India, 2018.

Which case promoted disclosure of income sources of candidates and specified family members? → Lok Prahari v. Union of India, 2018.

What is the easiest TNPSC distinction? → Lokpal = Union; Lokayukta = State; both are statutory anti-corruption ombudsman institutions, but Lokayukta structure depends on State law.
